::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py optimisation`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**How can we select parameters without searching an infinite number of possibilities?**

Gradient descent uses local sensitivity to improve a loss; Lagrange multipliers model equality constraints; convexity provides conditions under which local optima are globally meaningful. Optimisation connects the foundations to parameter fitting.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
\beta_{t+1}=\beta_t-\eta\nabla L(\beta_t)
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

For L(theta)=(theta-3)^2 at theta=0, a step with eta=0.1 moves to theta=0.6 and reduces the loss from 9 to 5.76. The step size and curvature jointly determine whether this trend continues.

## What to pay attention to

A feasible stationary point may not be a minimum without further conditions. Too large a learning rate can cause divergence.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
